title: Childhood immigrants reach journeyperson certification but face persistent, trade-specific earnings gaps that narrow with institutional and employment controls
source_unit: Statistics Canada, Early career economic outcomes of childhood immigrant and Canadian-born journeypersons in Canada
geography: Canada; childhood immigrants admitted at age 17 or younger and Canadian-born journeypersons certified from 2008 to 2018

observations.period: 2008–2018 certification cohorts; four years before certification through four years after

denominator.unit: journeypersons aged 18 to 54 in the linked administrative-data study

pre_certification_gap.unit: approximate Canadian-dollar median employment-income gap four years before certification, childhood immigrants lower

certification_gap.unit: approximate Canadian-dollar median employment-income gap in the certification year, childhood immigrants lower

post_certification_gap.unit: approximate Canadian-dollar median employment-income gap four years after certification, childhood immigrants lower

adjusted_gap.value: approximately 9% lower four years before certification and 6% to 7% lower at subsequent stages after sociodemographic, program, trade and employment controls

integration_route.value: early arrival and Canadian schooling do not by themselves erase occupational earnings inequality

observations.method: Linked Longitudinal Immigration Database, Registered Apprenticeship Information System and T1 Family File; annual employment incomes measured at five points around certification, with descriptive and OLS-adjusted comparisons.
observations.uncertainty: The study restricts analysis to people with complete tax records across observation periods and cannot establish that immigrant status causes the earnings differences; certification cohorts and trade selection are not random.
observations.subgroup: Childhood immigrants admitted before age 18 versus Canadian-born journeypersons, ages 18 to 54, certified through apprenticeship completion or trade qualification.
observations.counterinterpretation: Observed gaps may reflect trade composition, region, unionization, pensions, employment attachment, family conditions, employer sorting or unmeasured selection rather than a single integration barrier.

denominator.unit: journeypersons in the linked administrative-data study; trade-level estimates reported for selected occupations

higher_canadian_born_trades.value: Canadian-born journeypersons had higher median incomes in several industrial and mechanical trades, including heavy-duty equipment mechanics, construction millwrights, automotive service and HVAC trades

higher_childhood_immigrant_trades.value: Childhood immigrants had higher median incomes in selected construction trades, including cabinetmakers, carpenters, painters and decorators, roofers and shinglers, and some welding categories

largest_gap.value: heavy-duty equipment mechanics showed Canadian-born earnings advantages of approximately $6,700 to $10,500 across time points

occupation_route.value: aggregate integration statistics conceal occupation-specific labor-market mechanisms and bargaining conditions

observations.method: Trade-disaggregated median-income comparisons across five certification-relative time points using linked administrative records.
observations.uncertainty: Certified trade does not necessarily equal occupation at every observed time point; selected trade categories have different demand, union, regional and employment structures.
observations.subgroup: Childhood immigrant and Canadian-born journeypersons by certified trade.
observations.counterinterpretation: Trade-level differences can reflect who enters and remains in each trade, geographic labor demand, work hours, and employer composition rather than differential treatment within the same job.

observations.period: 2008–2018 certification cohorts; employment institutions and geographic mobility

denominator.unit: journeypersons in the linked administrative-data study

union_coverage.value: 33% of childhood immigrant journeypersons versus 46% of Canadian-born journeypersons were in unionized jobs

pension_coverage.value: 16% of childhood immigrant journeypersons versus 30% of Canadian-born journeypersons had a workplace pension plan

mobility_two_year.unit: approximate percent of childhood immigrant journeypersons moving province or territory two years after certification, versus about 5% of Canadian-born journeypersons

mobility_four_year.unit: approximate percent of childhood immigrant journeypersons moving province or territory four years after certification, versus about 6% of Canadian-born journeypersons

institutional_route.value: employment security and geographic opportunity are partly mediated by collective bargaining, pensions and mobility capacity

observations.method: Administrative employment, tax and mobility indicators linked to certification and immigrant status.
observations.uncertainty: Union and pension coverage are observed correlates, not experimentally assigned protections; interprovincial movement may reflect family, housing, trade demand, discrimination or preference.
observations.subgroup: Childhood immigrant and Canadian-born journeypersons after certification.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower observed mobility could indicate rootedness or different regional settlement patterns rather than reduced opportunity; employment institution measures do not capture informal bargaining or non-wage benefits.

observations.period: Two and four years after certification; income progression

denominator.unit: journeypersons in the linked administrative-data study with certification-relative income observations

two_year_growth.value: median employment income growth was 17% for childhood immigrants versus 15% for Canadian-born journeypersons two years after certification

four_year_growth.value: median employment income growth was 21% for childhood immigrants versus 19% for Canadian-born journeypersons four years after certification

adjusted_short_term.value: childhood immigrants had approximately 1% lower adjusted earnings growth two years after certification

adjusted_longer_term.value: the four-year adjusted earnings-growth difference was not statistically significant

trajectory_route.value: persistent level differences can coexist with broadly similar longer-run post-certification growth

observations.method: Certification-relative income progression estimates using linked administrative records and adjusted regression models.
observations.uncertainty: Growth from a lower starting point does not imply equal economic security; the study does not measure wealth, household needs, discrimination, job quality, health, or subjective belonging.
observations.subgroup: Childhood immigrant and Canadian-born journeypersons two and four years after certification, with trade-level heterogeneity.
observations.counterinterpretation: Similar growth rates may reflect convergence within selected trades or survivor composition; they do not show that earnings gaps disappear or that career advancement is equally reachable.

related_sources.claim: Official Statistics Canada catalogue entry and data-source description.
Earlier 2026 certification-stage study provides adjacent evidence on registration-to-certification gaps; it is not used as a substitute for the present earnings trajectory.
August 2026 sex-disaggregated companion study provides adjacent certification and earnings context.

boundary: This record adds a migration-and-work-integration route from childhood arrival and apprenticeship through certification, trade sorting, collective employment institutions, mobility, earnings and longer-run progression. It uses linked Canadian administrative data and longitudinal certification-relative comparisons, not a causal treatment effect, a complete measure of immigrant belonging, a household-welfare estimate, or evidence that any single policy explains the observed gaps.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official Statistics Canada article reviewed for release date, linked administrative datasets, sample, certification-relative earnings, trade heterogeneity, union and pension coverage, interprovincial mobility, regression results, progression and limitations.
